newsitem.title: JAPAN: Weak yen helps drive up Japan car exports.
newsitem.headline: Weak yen helps drive up Japan car exports.

text.p: Japan's car exports surged last month as shipments shifted into higher gear to meet demand generated by the strong yen, industry data showed on Wednesday.

Japan's vehicle exports rose by 18.5 percent in April from a year earlier to 362,416 units -- the 11th increase in a row on a year-on-year basis -- helped by the weaker yen, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association (JAMA) said.

But industry executives played down the significance of the figures and the possibility that the export boom could inflame trade tension with the United States, which has warned Japan against relying on exports to boost its economy.
They said the scale of the rise was exaggerated by particularly low exports a year earlier.

Exports to the United States rose 11.7 percent to 100,966 units, less than the overall rate. Exports to Europe rose by 26.7 percent to 97,706 units, while the strongest growth was seen in exports to Africa and Latin America.

The strong export growth at the carmakers risks re-igniting trade tension with the United States, which warned this week that trade ties with Japan were entering a "delicate and potentially difficult" period.

U.S. government figures released last Wednesday showed the U.S. trade deficit with Japan grew 8.3 percent in March to $4.6 billion, with American car industry officials complaining that the weak yen is hurting U.S. carmakers.
A JAMA offical said that in April the volume of Japan's car exports to all geographical regions rose across the board for the first time since 1981.
In April 1996, car exports had dropped 15.7 percent as a strong yen held back Japanese exporters.

The industry official said Japan's overall car exports in the fiscal year to March 1998 were likely to be flat compared with the previous year, as exports have been running at a high level since last June. Exports rose rose 6.2 percent to 3.37 million units in 1996/97.

"Trade friction between the United States and Japan is unlikely this year because the Big Three's businesses are in good shape. And we do not have the excess capacity to boost exports sharply," a spokesman for Toyota Motor Corp said.
Toyota's exports in April rose 1.8 percent to 118,423 units after a decline of 1.1 percent in March, although its exports to the United States fell four percent in April.
Toyota said the rise in its exports would remain moderate, despite the weaker yen.

Toyota, Japan's biggest carmaker, has said it will cut vehicle exports to the United States to 480,000 units in 1997/98 from an actual 490,000 a year earlier, while its overall exports will rise to 1.40 million units from 1.31 million a year earlier.
Nissan Motor Co's April exports rose a steep 32.7 percent to 58,512 units but the company said this reflected unusually low exports in the prior period.
Nissan has predicted its overall exports will rise 3.6 percent to 620,000 units in 1997/98, mainly due to higher shipments to the Asian market.
Honda said last week it expected its car exports to rise 15.1 percent from a year earlier to 470,000 units in 1997/98.
It is aiming to raise car exports to the United States to 240,000 units this year from 183,700 a year earlier, due to strong demand for compact and light sport-utility models.
Honda said its North American production will rise to 820,000 units in 1997/98 from 798,000 a year earlier.
